title: Μνηστήρων βουλή
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Telemachus answers Odysseus’s plan to test the household: he is not slack, but going round the farms to try each man will gain them nothing while the suitors eat the goods, so they should find out only which of the women dishonour Odysseus. Meanwhile Telemachus’s ship puts in, and a herald from the crew and Eumaeus, meeting on the way, bring the same news to Penelope. The suitors, downcast, come out before the doors, and Eurymachus proposes to send a ship to call the ambushers home; but Amphinomus sees the ship already in the harbour. In the assembly place Antinous says that the lookouts and the ship had kept watch in vain, for a power carried Telemachus home. He urges that they seize and kill him in the country or on the road before he rouses the people against them, share his goods, and give the house to his mother and her husband; or, if they would rather let him live, that they stop eating his goods and court Penelope each from his own hall, with gifts.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσεφώνεε φαίδιμος υἱός
ὦ πάτερ, ἦ τοι ἐμὸν θυμὸν καὶ ἔπειτά γ’, ὀΐω,
γνώσεαι·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ apameibomenos prosephōnee phaidimos huios
ō pater, ē toi emon thymon kai epeita g’, oïō,
gnōseai·
sentences.i: In answer the glorious son spoke to him: “Father, I think you will come to know my heart, even in the time to come;
sentences.n: τὸν is the old demonstrative, ‘him’, Odysseus, whose speech the previous part ends on; in Homer the forms that look like the article are pronouns. ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is a present participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and προσεφώνεε ‘spoke to’ is an imperfect with the uncontracted ending -εε (Attic προσεφώνει). φαίδιμος is a stock epithet, translated ‘glorious’ every time, and υἱός ‘son’ is Telemachus, left unnamed because the line points back to the speech just made. The archive prints no stop at the end of this line,, and the speech itself begins with the next word. ὦ πάτερ is ‘O father’, and ἦ τοι ‘truly’ opens Telemachus’s answer to the plan on which the previous part ends, that the two of them should test the household. ἐμὸν θυμὸν ‘my heart’ is the object of γνώσεαι ‘you will come to know’, the epic uncontracted second-person future (Attic γνώσῃ). καὶ ἔπειτά γ’ is ‘even afterward, in time to come’, and ὀΐω ‘I think’ is slipped in as a parenthesis. θυμός, the seat of feeling and courage, is ‘heart’ throughout.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι χαλιφροσύναι γέ μ’ ἔχουσιν·
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti chaliphrosynai ge m’ echousin·
sentences.l: for in no way do slacknesses-of-mind hold me;
sentences.i: for no slackness of mind has any hold on me;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι is ‘for not at all’. The plural χαλιφροσύναι ‘slacknesses of mind’ is built from χαλι- ‘loose, slack’ and φρήν ‘mind’; the word is rare, and the sense is taken from its parts. γέ μ’ is γε με, ‘me, at least’, and ἔχουσιν is plural to agree with the plural subject, so the Greek says that slacknesses do not hold him. The unit ends at Murray’s ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ τοι τόδε κέρδος ἐγὼν ἔσσεσθαι ὀΐω
ἡμῖν ἀμφοτέροισι·
sentences.tr:
all’ ou toi tode kerdos egōn essesthai oïō
hēmin amphoteroisi·
sentences.l:
But not, mark you, this gain do I think will be
for us both;
sentences.i: But I do not think this will be a gain for the two of us;
sentences.n: τόδε ‘this’ refers to the plan of testing the household. οὔ τοι is ‘not, I tell you’, ἐγὼν is ἐγώ with the movable -ν, and ὀΐω ‘I think’ takes the infinitive ἔσσεσθαι, the epic future infinitive of εἰμί (Attic ἔσεσθαι), ‘will be’. κέρδος is ‘gain, advantage’, and ἡμῖν ἀμφοτέροισι is a dative in -οισι, ‘for us both’.

sentences.t: σὲ δὲ φράζεσθαι ἄνωγα.
sentences.tr: se de phrazesthai anōga.
sentences.l: but you to take thought I bid.
sentences.i: but I urge you to think it over.
sentences.n: σὲ is the accusative ‘you’, the subject of the infinitive φράζεσθαι ‘to take thought, to consider’ (middle of φράζω). ἄνωγα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I bid, I urge’. After the ano teleia the clause stands alone as a short, firm request.

sentences.t:
δηθὰ γὰρ αὔτως εἴσῃ ἑκάστου πειρητίζων,
ἔργα μετερχόμενος·
sentences.tr:
dētha gar autōs eisēi hekastou peirētizōn,
erga meterchomenos·
sentences.l:
for long, just so, you will be going about, testing each man,
going after their works;
sentences.i: for you will simply be going about for a long time, testing each man and going after one man’s work and then another’s;
sentences.n: δηθά is ‘for a long time’ and αὔτως ‘just so’, that is, to no effect, with nothing gained. εἴσῃ is a rare second-person future, ‘you will go about’, and the sense is taken from the context. ἑκάστου πειρητίζων is ‘testing each man’, πειρητίζω ‘try, test’ taking the genitive of the person tried; ἔργα μετερχόμενος is ‘going after their works’, μετέρχομαι ‘go after, go among’, so that Telemachus pictures Odysseus calling at one man’s work after another’s.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἐν μεγάροισιν ἕκηλοι
χρήματα δαρδάπτουσιν ὑπέρβιον οὐδ’ ἔπι φειδώ.
sentences.tr:
toi d’ en megaroisin hekēloi
chrēmata dardaptousin hyperbion oud’ epi pheidō.
sentences.l:
while they in the halls at ease
goods devour with exceeding violence, and there is no sparing.
sentences.i: while they, at their ease in the halls, devour the goods with exceeding violence, and there is no sparing.
sentences.n: τοί is ‘they’, an article-form used as a pronoun, the suitors. ἕκηλοι ‘at ease’ and the adverb ὑπέρβιον ‘with exceeding violence’ (from ὑπέρβιος ‘overbearing’) say how they eat, and δαρδάπτουσιν is ‘devour’. οὐδ’ ἔπι φειδώ is ‘nor is there sparing’: ἔπι is the preposition ἐπί with its accent thrown back, standing for ἔπεστι ‘is there’. μεγάροισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, ‘in the halls’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοί σε γυναῖκας ἐγὼ δεδάασθαι ἄνωγα,
αἵ τέ σ’ ἀτιμάζουσι καὶ αἳ νηλείτιδές εἰσιν·
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi se gynaikas egō dedaasthai anōga,
hai te s’ atimazousi kai hai nēleitides eisin·
sentences.l:
But truly the women I bid you to learn about,
both those who dishonour you and who are guiltless;
sentences.i: But it is the women I bid you find out about: which of them dishonour you, and which are guiltless;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι is ‘but truly’. δεδάασθαι is a reduplicated epic infinitive of δάω ‘learn, find out about’, with γυναῖκας ‘the women’ as its object; ἄνωγα ‘I bid’ governs it, and σε ‘you’ is the person bidden. αἵ τέ σ’ ἀτιμάζουσι is ‘who dishonour you’: αἵ is a relative, an article-form, τέ is the epic particle, and σ’ is σε elided; ἀτιμάζω ‘dishonour’. νηλείτιδες is ‘guiltless’, and καὶ αἳ … εἰσιν is ‘and who are’, so the women fall into two groups.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρῶν δ’ οὐκ ἂν ἐγώ γε κατὰ σταθμοὺς ἐθέλοιμι
ἡμέας πειράζειν, ἀλλ’ ὕστερα ταῦτα πένεσθαι,
εἰ ἐτεόν γέ τι οἶσθα Διὸς τέρας αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
andrōn d’ ouk an egō ge kata stathmous etheloimi
hēmeas peirazein, all’ hystera tauta penesthai,
ei eteon ge ti oistha Dios teras aigiochoio.
sentences.l:
But of the men — I would not wish, among the steadings,
us to test, but these things afterwards to busy ourselves with,
if truly you know some portent of aegis-bearing Zeus.”
sentences.i: As for the men, I would not wish us to go testing them through the steadings; that can be our business afterwards, if you truly know some portent from aegis-bearing Zeus.”
sentences.n: ἀνδρῶν δ’ is ‘but as for the men’, the genitive set first to contrast with the women. ἐθέλοιμι is the optative with ἄν, so οὐκ ἂν … ἐθέλοιμι is ‘I would not wish’; ἡμέας ‘us’ (= ἡμᾶς) is the subject of πειράζειν ‘to test’, and κατὰ σταθμούς is ‘through the steadings’, the farm-buildings. ἀλλ’ ὕστερα ταῦτα πένεσθαι goes on with the same wish, ‘but to busy ourselves with these things later’ (πένομαι ‘busy oneself with’). εἰ ἐτεόν γέ τι οἶσθα is ‘if you truly know anything’, and Διὸς τέρας is ‘a portent from Zeus’; the meaning of αἰγιόχοιο, a stock epithet of Zeus in the genitive in -οιο, is disputed, and ‘aegis-bearing’ follows the traditional reading. The closing quotation mark ends Telemachus’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
ἡ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτ’ Ἰθάκηνδε κατήγετο νηῦς εὐεργής,
ἣ φέρε Τηλέμαχον Πυλόθεν καὶ πάντας ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
hē d’ ar’ epeit’ Ithakēnde katēgeto nēus euergēs,
hē phere Tēlemachon Pylothen kai pantas hetairous.
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
and she, then, to Ithaca was putting in, the ship well-made,
which was carrying Telemachus from Pylos and all his companions.
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, and meanwhile the well-made ship was putting in at Ithaca, the ship that was bringing Telemachus from Pylos with all his companions.
sentences.n: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον is a stock line that closes a conversation: οἱ μέν ‘they’ are Odysseus and Telemachus in the hut, set against the crew of the ship that the next lines bring into view, and ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’. The ἡ of ἡ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτ’ is a pronoun, ‘she’, the ship; κατήγετο is the imperfect middle of κατάγω, ‘was being brought down’, said of a ship ‘putting in’ to land. Ἰθάκηνδε ‘to Ithaca’ has the -δε of direction, and νηῦς is the epic nominative of ναῦς. εὐεργής is ‘well-made’; ἣ φέρε is ‘which was carrying’, an unaugmented imperfect, and Πυλόθεν ‘from Pylos’ has the -θεν of source.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὅτε δὴ λιμένος πολυβενθέος ἐντὸς ἵκοντο,
νῆα μὲν οἵ γε μέλαιναν ἐπ’ ἠπείροιο ἔρυσσαν,
τεύχεα δέ σφ’ ἀπένεικαν ὑπέρθυμοι θεράποντες,
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐς Κλυτίοιο φέρον περικαλλέα δῶρα.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē limenos polybentheos entos hikonto,
nēa men hoi ge melainan ep’ ēpeiroio eryssan,
teuchea de sph’ apeneikan hyperthymoi therapontes,
autika d’ es Klytioio pheron perikallea dōra.
sentences.l:
And they, when indeed within the very deep harbour they had come,
the black ship, they for their part, onto the dry land drew,
and their gear carried off the high-spirited attendants,
and at once to Clytius’ they carried the very fair gifts.
sentences.i: When they had come inside the deep harbour, they drew the black ship up onto the dry land, and the high-spirited attendants carried their gear away, and at once they took the very fair gifts to Clytius’ house.
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’, the ship’s company, and ἵκοντο is an unaugmented past tense of ἱκνέομαι ‘come, arrive’. λιμένος πολυβενθέος ἐντός is ‘inside the very deep harbour’ (ἐντός takes the genitive; πολυβενθής is πολύ- ‘very’ + βένθος ‘depth’). ἔρυσσαν ‘drew’ is unaugmented, and ἐπ’ ἠπείροιο ‘onto the dry land’ has a genitive in -οιο (= -ου); νῆα μέλαιναν is ‘the black ship’. τεύχεα ‘gear’ is the object of ἀπένεικαν, the epic aorist of ἀποφέρω without the augment (the augmented form is ἀπήνεικαν), and σφ’ is σφι ‘for them’. ὑπέρθυμοι θεράποντες ‘high-spirited attendants’ is a stock phrase, translated in full each time. ἐς Κλυτίοιο is ‘to the house of Clytius’, the word for ‘house’ being understood; περικαλλέα ‘very fair’ is περί- ‘very’ + κάλλος ‘beauty’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ κήρυκα πρόεσαν δόμον εἰς Ὀδυσῆος,
ἀγγελίην ἐρέοντα περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ,
sentences.tr:
autar kēryka proesan domon eis Odysēos,
angeliēn ereonta periphroni Pēnelopeiēi,
sentences.l:
But a herald they sent forth to the house of Odysseus,
news to tell to circumspect Penelope,
sentences.i: They sent a herald to the house of Odysseus to take the news to circumspect Penelope,
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns the story from the harbour to the town. πρόεσαν is the aorist of προΐημι, ‘they sent forth’, and κήρυκα ‘herald’ is its object; εἰς stands after its noun in δόμον εἰς Ὀδυσῆος ‘to the house of Odysseus’, with Ὀδυσῆος a metrical variant of Ὀδυσσῆος. ἐρέοντα is the future participle of ἐρέω ‘I shall say’, expressing purpose, ‘to tell’, and ἀγγελίην ‘news’ is its object. περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ is the dative of Πηνελόπεια, and περίφρων ‘circumspect’ is her stock epithet. The unit stops at the comma because the sentence would otherwise run past four lines.

sentences.t:
οὕνεκα Τηλέμαχος μὲν ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ, νῆα δ’ ἀνώγει
ἄστυδ’ ἀποπλείειν, ἵνα μὴ δείσασ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ἰφθίμη βασίλεια τέρεν κατὰ δάκρυον εἴβοι
τὼ δὲ συναντήτην κῆρυξ καὶ δῖος ὑφορβὸς
τῆς αὐτῆς ἕνεκ’ ἀγγελίης, ἐρέοντε γυναικί.
sentences.tr:
houneka Tēlemachos men ep’ agrou, nēa d’ anōgei
astyd’ apopleiein, hina mē deisas’ eni thymōi
iphthimē basileia teren kata dakryon eiboi
tō de synantētēn kēryx kai dios hyphorbos
tēs autēs henek’ angeliēs, ereonte gynaiki.
sentences.l:
that Telemachus was in the country, and the ship he had bidden
to sail off to the town, so that she not, afraid in her heart,
the mighty queen, a tender tear let fall.
And the two met, the herald and the heavenly swineherd,
on account of the same news, both to tell it to the woman.
sentences.i: that Telemachus was in the country and had told the ship to sail on to the town, so that the mighty queen would not take fright in her heart and shed a tender tear. The herald and the heavenly swineherd met one another, each on the same errand, to tell the same news to the woman of the house.
sentences.n: οὕνεκα, the same as ὅτι, introduces what the message is. μὲν … δέ sets Telemachus ‘in the country’ (ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ) against the ship, which ἀνώγει ‘he had bidden’ (the past of ἄνωγα) to ἀποπλείειν ‘sail off’ to the town (ἄστυδ’ has the -δε of direction). ἵνα μὴ … εἴβοι is a purpose clause with the optative: ‘so that she might not let fall’. δείσασ’ is the aorist participle ‘having become afraid’; ἰφθίμη βασίλεια ‘mighty queen’ is Penelope with a stock epithet, translated each time; and κατὰ … εἴβοι ‘let fall’ is tmesis, the preverb κατά standing apart from its verb with τέρεν … δάκρυον ‘a tender tear’ between them. The archive prints no stop after this line; the unit ends where the sentence does. τὼ and συναντήτην are dual forms: ‘the two met’ (συναντάω ‘meet’), the herald and the swineherd. δῖος ὑφορβός is ‘the heavenly swineherd’: δῖος is a stock epithet, ‘heavenly’ every time, and ὑφορβός ‘swineherd’ (ὑπό + φέρβω ‘feed’) is the same man whom 338 calls συβώτης. τῆς αὐτῆς ἕνεκ’ ἀγγελίης is ‘for the sake of the same news’ (ἕνεκα follows its genitive), and ἐρέοντε is the dual of the future participle ‘about to tell’. γυναικί ‘to the woman’ is Penelope, left unnamed.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκοντο δόμον θείου βασιλῆος,
κῆρυξ μέν ῥα μέσῃσι μετὰ δμῳῇσιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ hikonto domon theiou basilēos,
kēryx men rha mesēisi meta dmōiēisin eeipen·
sentences.l:
But when indeed they came to the house of the divine king,
the herald, then, in the midst of the maidservants spoke:
sentences.i: But when they came to the house of the divine king, the herald spoke out among the maids:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκοντο is ‘but when indeed they came’ (ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle of sequence), and δόμον θείου βασιλῆος is ‘the house of the divine king’, with βασιλῆος the Ionic genitive (Attic βασιλέως); θεῖος is ‘divine’, and the king is Odysseus. μέσῃσι μετὰ δμῳῇσιν is ‘in the midst of the maidservants’: μετά takes the dative, and both words have the dative plural in -ῃσι(ν) (Attic -αις). ἔειπεν ‘spoke’ is an aorist of εἶπον with its epic doubled vowel. κῆρυξ μέν ῥα points ahead to the swineherd, who speaks next.

sentences.t: ἤδη τοι, βασίλεια, φίλος πάϊς εἰλήλουθε.
sentences.tr: ēdē toi, basileia, philos païs eilēlouthe.
sentences.l: “Already, to you, queen, the dear son has come.”
sentences.i: “Your dear son has already come, queen.”
sentences.n: ἤδη ‘already’ comes first, and τοι is either the dative ‘to you’ or a particle of emphasis; the translation takes it as ‘you’. βασίλεια is the vocative ‘queen’. φίλος πάϊς is ‘dear son’, πάϊς being the epic form of παῖς, and εἰλήλουθε is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘has come’, with the reduplication of the epic form (Attic ἐλήλυθε). The herald’s announcement is one line long, and the closing quotation mark ends it.

sentences.t:
Πηνελοπείῃ δ’ εἶπε συβώτης ἄγχι παραστὰς
πάνθ’ ὅσα οἱ φίλος υἱὸς ἀνώγει μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
Pēnelopeiēi d’ eipe sybōtēs anchi parastas
panth’ hosa hoi philos huios anōgei mythēsasthai.
sentences.l:
And to Penelope spoke the swineherd, standing close by,
all that her dear son had bidden him to tell.
sentences.i: Standing close beside Penelope, the swineherd told her all that her dear son had bidden him tell.
sentences.n: Πηνελοπείῃ is the dative of Πηνελόπεια, and συβώτης is ‘swineherd’. ἄγχι παραστάς is ‘standing close beside’: the aorist participle of παρίστημι with ἄγχι ‘near’. πάνθ’ ὅσα is ‘everything that’; οἱ is ‘her’, read with φίλος υἱός ‘dear son’, and ἀνώγει ‘had bidden’ takes the infinitive μυθήσασθαι ‘to tell’, the person bidden being understood. What the herald announced aloud in one line, the swineherd gives here in reported form.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πᾶσαν ἐφημοσύνην ἀπέειπε,
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεναι μεθ’ ὕας, λίπε δ’ ἕρκεά τε μέγαρόν τε.
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē pasan ephēmosynēn apeeipe,
bē rh’ imenai meth’ hyas, lipe d’ herkea te megaron te.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the whole behest he had delivered,
he set out to go among the swine, and left the enclosures and the hall.
sentences.i: When he had delivered the whole message, he set out for his swine, and left the courtyard and the hall.
sentences.n: ἐφημοσύνη is ‘behest, instruction’, the thing laid on him to say, and ἀπέειπε is an aorist of ἀπεῖπον, ‘delivered, told in full’. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεναι is ‘he set out to go’: βῆ is an unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, ῥ’ is ῥα, and ἴμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’. μεθ’ ὕας is ‘after the swine’ (μετά takes the accusative; ὕας is the accusative plural of ὗς), and ἕρκεά τε μέγαρόν τε ‘both the enclosures and the hall’ uses ἕρκεα, the plural of ἕρκος ‘fence, enclosure’, for the walled court.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρες δ’ ἀκάχοντο κατήφησάν τ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
ἐκ δ’ ἦλθον μεγάροιο παρὲκ μέγα τειχίον αὐλῆς,
αὐτοῦ δὲ προπάροιθε θυράων ἑδριόωντο.
sentences.tr:
mnēstēres d’ akachonto katēphēsan t’ eni thymōi,
ek d’ ēlthon megaroio parek mega teichion aulēs,
autou de proparoithe thyraōn hedrioōnto.
sentences.l:
But the suitors were grieved, and downcast in their heart,
and out they went from the hall, past the great wall of the yard,
and right there, before the doors, they sat.
sentences.i: But the suitors were grieved and downcast in their hearts, and they went out of the hall, past the great wall of the yard, and sat down right there before the doors.
sentences.n: ἀκάχοντο ‘were grieved’ is a past tense, middle in form, of ἀκαχίζω, and κατήφησαν ‘were downcast’ is the aorist of κατηφέω; ἐνὶ θυμῷ is ‘in heart’, ἐνί being ἐν. ἐκ δ’ ἦλθον is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from its verb (ἐξῆλθον ‘went out’), and μεγάροιο ‘of the hall’ has the genitive in -οιο. παρέκ ‘past’ takes the accusative, μέγα τειχίον αὐλῆς is ‘the great wall of the yard’, and τειχίον is a diminutive form of τεῖχος ‘wall’. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’, προπάροιθε takes the genitive θυράων (Ionic -άων for -ῶν), and ἑδριόωντο is the imperfect of ἑδριάομαι ‘sit’, uncontracted.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Εὐρύμαχος, Πολύβου πάϊς, ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν·
sentences.tr: toisin d’ Eurymachos, Polybou païs, ērch’ agoreuein·
sentences.l: And among them Eurymachus, Polybus’ son, began to speak-in-assembly:
sentences.i: Eurymachus, son of Polybus, was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is the pronoun in the dative, ‘among them’. Εὐρύμαχος, Πολύβου πάϊς is ‘Eurymachus, son of Polybus’, πάϊς being the epic παῖς ‘son’. ἦρχ’ is ἦρχε, the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘begin’, and it takes the infinitive ἀγορεύειν ‘to speak’; ἀγορεύω is properly ‘speak in assembly, address a gathering’, and the suitors are sitting before the doors, not in a formal assembly. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, ἦ μέγα ἔργον ὑπερφιάλως τετέλεσται
Τηλεμάχῳ ὁδὸς ἥδε·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi, ē mega ergon hyperphialōs tetelestai
Tēlemachōi hodos hēde·
sentences.l:
“O friends, truly a great deed has been done overweeningly —
this journey of Telemachus’s;
sentences.i: “Friends, truly this journey of Telemachus’s is a great deed, overweeningly accomplished;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is ‘O friends’, and ἦ is ‘truly’. ἔργον ‘deed’ is the subject of τετέλεσται, the perfect passive of τελέω ‘accomplish’, ‘has been accomplished’, and ὑπερφιάλως is the adverb of ὑπερφίαλος ‘overweening’. Τηλεμάχῳ ὁδὸς ἥδε is ‘this journey for Telemachus’, which English says as ‘this journey of Telemachus’s’; the phrase says what the great deed is. Eurymachus means the suitors’ failure to stop it.

sentences.t: φάμεν δέ οἱ οὐ τελέεσθαι.
sentences.tr: phamen de hoi ou teleesthai.
sentences.l: yet we said that it would not be accomplished.
sentences.i: and yet we said it would come to nothing.
sentences.n: φάμεν is the first person plural of φημί ‘say’, an imperfect without the augment, ‘we said’. οἱ is ‘as for him’, and τελέεσθαι is the future infinitive passive of τελέω, uncontracted, ‘would be accomplished’; with οὐ it reports what the suitors had claimed, that the journey would come to nothing.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῆα μέλαιναν ἐρύσσομεν ἥ τις ἀρίστη,
ἐς δ’ ἐρέτας ἁλιῆας ἀγείρομεν, οἵ κε τάχιστα
κείνοις ἀγγείλωσι θοῶς οἶκόνδε νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
all’ age nēa melainan eryssomen hē tis aristē,
es d’ eretas haliēas ageiromen, hoi ke tachista
keinois angeilōsi thoōs oikonde neesthai.
sentences.l:
But come, let us draw down a black ship, the best there is,
and let us gather in rowers, sea-men, who most quickly
to those men may announce swiftly to come home.”
sentences.i: But come, let us launch a black ship, the best there is, and gather seamen to row her, who can most quickly bring those men word to come home.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and ἐρύσσομεν and ἀγείρομεν are first-person plural subjunctives in the short-vowel form, ‘let us draw down’, ‘let us gather’. ἥ τις ἀρίστη is ‘whichever is best’. ἐς … ἀγείρομεν is tmesis (ἐσαγείρομεν, ‘gather in’), with ἐρέτας ἁλιῆας ‘oarsmen, seamen’ as its object (ἐρέτης ‘rower’, ἁλιεύς ‘seaman’, accusative plural). οἵ κε … ἀγγείλωσι is a relative clause with κε and the aorist subjunctive, ‘who may report’; κείνοις is ‘to those men’, the ambush party, and νέεσθαι ‘to come, to go’ (uncontracted) with οἶκόνδε ‘homeward’ says what the word is. θοῶς is ‘swiftly’. The closing quotation mark ends Eurymachus’s speech.

sentences.t:
οὔ πω πᾶν εἴρηθ’, ὅτ’ ἄρ’ Ἀμφίνομος ἴδε νῆα,
στρεφθεὶς ἐκ χώρης, λιμένος πολυβενθέος ἐντός,
ἱστία τε στέλλοντας ἐρετμά τε χερσὶν ἔχοντας.
sentences.tr:
ou pō pan eirēth’, hot’ ar’ Amphinomos ide nēa,
strephtheis ek chōrēs, limenos polybentheos entos,
histia te stellontas eretma te chersin echontas.
sentences.l:
Not yet had everything been said, when Amphinomus saw the ship,
turning round from his place, inside the very deep harbour,
(men) furling the sails and holding oars in their hands.
sentences.i: He had not yet finished speaking when Amphinomus, turning round in his place, saw the ship inside the deep harbour, and the men furling the sails and holding oars in their hands.
sentences.n: οὔ πω πᾶν εἴρηθ’ is ‘not yet had everything been said’, εἴρηθ’ being an elided form of the verb ‘say’ (εἴρω). Ἀμφίνομος ‘Amphinomus’ is a suitor, named here for the first time in this part. ἴδε is ‘saw’, unaugmented, and στρεφθείς is the aorist passive participle of στρέφω, ‘having turned round’; χώρης is the Ionic genitive of χώρα, ‘place’. λιμένος πολυβενθέος ἐντός is the same phrase as in 324. στέλλοντας and ἔχοντας are masculine accusative plural participles, ‘furling’ and ‘holding’, so they belong to the crew, who are not named; ἐρετμά is the plural of ἐρετμόν ‘oar’.

sentences.t: ἡδὺ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐκγελάσας μετεφώνεεν οἷς ἑτάροισι·
sentences.tr: hēdy d’ ar’ ekgelasas metephōneen hois hetaroisi·
sentences.l: And sweetly, then, laughing out, he spoke among his own companions:
sentences.i: With a pleasant laugh he spoke among his own companions:
sentences.n: ἡδύ is the neuter of ἡδύς ‘sweet’ used as an adverb, ‘sweetly, pleasantly’, and ἐκγελάσας is the aorist participle of ἐκγελάω ‘laugh out’. μετεφώνεεν is ‘spoke among’ (μετα- + φωνέω), an imperfect with the uncontracted ending -εεν. οἷς is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative ‘whom’, and ἑτάροισι is the dative plural of ἑταῖρος ‘companion’; the companions are the other suitors.

sentences.t: μή τιν’ ἔτ’ ἀγγελίην ὀτρύνομεν·
sentences.tr: mē tin’ et’ angeliēn otrynomen·
sentences.l: “Let us not any longer urge on any news;
sentences.i: “Let us not send on any further news;
sentences.n: μή with a first-person plural subjunctive (ὀτρύνομεν) makes a negative exhortation, ‘let us not’. ὀτρύνω is ‘urge on, send forward’, and ἀγγελίην ‘news’ is its object, with τιν’ ‘any’ and ἔτ’ ‘any longer’. The ano teleia closes the unit here, and the reason follows in the next.

sentences.t: οἵδε γὰρ ἔνδον.
sentences.tr: hoide gar endon.
sentences.l: for these men are within.
sentences.i: for these men are inside.
sentences.n: οἵδε is ‘these here’, nominative plural of ὅδε, pointing to the crew he has just seen, and ἔνδον is ‘within’: inside the harbour, as the previous sentence says. The line does not say more than that.

sentences.t:
ἤ τίς σφιν τόδ’ ἔειπε θεῶν, ἢ εἴσιδον αὐτοὶ
νῆα παρερχομένην, τὴν δ’ οὐκ ἐδύναντο κιχῆναι.
sentences.tr:
ē tis sphin tod’ eeipe theōn, ē eisidon autoi
nēa parerchomenēn, tēn d’ ouk edynanto kichēnai.
sentences.l:
Either one of the gods told them this, or themselves they saw
the ship passing by, but her they were not able to overtake.”
sentences.i: Either one of the gods told them this, or they saw the ship going past for themselves and could not overtake her.”
sentences.n: ἤ … ἢ is ‘either … or’. τίς … θεῶν is ‘some one of the gods’ (a partitive genitive), σφιν is the dative plural ‘to them’, and ἔειπε is the aorist of εἶπον. εἴσιδον is ‘saw’ and αὐτοί ‘themselves’; νῆα παρερχομένην is ‘the ship going past’ (παρέρχομαι ‘go by’). τὴν δ’ οὐκ ἐδύναντο κιχῆναι is ‘and her they could not overtake’, κιχῆναι being the aorist infinitive of κιχάνω. The Greek does not say whose ship is meant, and νῆα is simply ‘the ship’. The closing quotation mark ends Amphinomus’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἀνστάντες ἔβαν ἐπὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης,
αἶψα δὲ νῆα μέλαιναν ἐπ’ ἠπείροιο ἔρυσσαν,
τεύχεα δέ σφ’ ἀπένεικαν ὑπέρθυμοι θεράποντες.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ anstantes eban epi thina thalassēs,
aipsa de nēa melainan ep’ ēpeiroio eryssan,
teuchea de sph’ apeneikan hyperthymoi therapontes.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they, rising up, went to the shore of the sea,
and quickly the black ship onto the dry land they drew,
and their gear carried off the high-spirited attendants.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they rose and went down to the shore of the sea, and quickly drew the black ship up onto the dry land, and the high-spirited attendants carried their gear away.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο). ἀνστάντες is ‘having risen’, the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι with its preverb shortened, and ἔβαν is the epic aorist ‘went’ (Attic ἔβησαν). θῖνα θαλάσσης is ‘the shore of the sea’, and αἶψα ‘quickly’. The last two lines repeat 325–326 almost word for word: what Telemachus’s crew did on landing, the suitors now do.

sentences.t:
αὐτοὶ δ’ εἰς ἀγορὴν κίον ἀθρόοι, οὐδέ τιν’ ἄλλον
εἴων οὔτε νέων μεταΐζειν οὔτε γερόντων.
sentences.tr:
autoi d’ eis agorēn kion athrooi, oude tin’ allon
eiōn oute neōn metaïzein oute gerontōn.
sentences.l:
And they themselves to the assembly went, all together, and no one else
they allowed to sit among them, neither of the young nor of the old.
sentences.i: They themselves went to the assembly in a body, and would let no one else, young or old, sit with them.
sentences.n: αὐτοὶ δ’ is ‘and they themselves’, and κίον is ‘went’, the epic imperfect of κίω without the augment. ἀγορήν is ‘assembly’, here the place where men meet, and ἀθρόοι is ‘in a crowd, all together’. εἴων is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, and μεταΐζειν is ‘to sit among, to sit with’ (μετά + ἵζω; the sense is taken from its parts). νέων and γερόντων are genitives plural, ‘of the young men’ and ‘of the old men’, after οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’ and τιν’ ἄλλον ‘anyone else’.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀντίνοος μετέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.tr: toisin d’ Antinoos metephē, Eupeitheos huios·
sentences.l: Among them then spoke Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Among them Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke:
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is ‘among them’, the pronoun in the dative, and μετέφη is ‘spoke among’, an aorist of μετάφημι. Ἀντίνοος, Εὐπείθεος υἱός is ‘Antinous, son of Eupeithes’, with Εὐπείθεος the genitive of the father’s name. The unit ends at the ano teleia, and the speech follows.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι, ὡς τόνδ’ ἄνδρα θεοὶ κακότητος ἔλυσαν.
sentences.tr: ō popoi, hōs tond’ andra theoi kakotētos elysan.
sentences.l: “Ah! how this man the gods have released from evil.
sentences.i: “Ah, how the gods have delivered this man from evil.
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is a cry of dismay, ‘Ah!’, the house rendering. ὡς is exclamatory, ‘how!’, and τόνδ’ ἄνδρα is ‘this man’, who is Telemachus, not yet named. κακότητος ‘from evil’ is a genitive of separation, and ἔλυσαν is the aorist of λύω ‘release, set free’.

sentences.t:
ἤματα μὲν σκοποὶ ἷζον ἐπ’ ἄκριας ἠνεμοέσσας
αἰὲν ἐπασσύτεροι·
sentences.tr:
ēmata men skopoi hizon ep’ akrias ēnemoessas
aien epassyteroi·
sentences.l:
By day the lookouts sat upon the windy hilltops,
always one close upon another;
sentences.i: By day lookouts sat on the windy hilltops, always one man after another;
sentences.n: ἤματα is the accusative plural of ἦμαρ ‘day’, used adverbially, ‘by day’. σκοποί is ‘lookouts’ (σκοπός ‘one who looks out’), and ἷζον is the imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit’. ἄκριας ἠνεμοέσσας is ‘windy hilltops’ (ἄκρις ‘hilltop’, ἠνεμόεις ‘windy’, from ἄνεμος ‘wind’), the accusative plural in -ας. αἰέν is ‘always’, and ἐπασσύτεροι is ‘one close upon another’, said of men who follow one another in turn.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἠελίῳ καταδύντι
οὔ ποτ’ ἐπ’ ἠπείρου νύκτ’ ἄσαμεν, ἀλλ’ ἐνὶ πόντῳ
νηῒ θοῇ πλείοντες ἐμίμνομεν Ἠῶ δῖαν,
sentences.tr:
hama d’ ēeliōi katadynti
ou pot’ ep’ ēpeirou nykt’ asamen, all’ eni pontōi
nēï thoēi pleiontes emimnomen Ēō dian,
sentences.l:
and at the setting of the sun
never on the dry land did we pass the night, but on the open-sea
in a swift ship, sailing, we waited for heavenly Dawn,
sentences.i: and at sunset we never spent the night on dry land, but stayed out on the open sea in a swift ship, sailing about and waiting for heavenly Dawn,
sentences.n: ἅμα δ’ ἠελίῳ καταδύντι is ‘and at the setting of the sun’, a dative absolute: ἅμα takes the dative, and καταδύντι is the aorist participle of καταδύω ‘sink, set’. ἄσαμεν is the aorist of ἄω ‘pass the night, sleep’, ἐπ’ ἠπείρου is ‘on the dry land’, and ἐνὶ πόντῳ is ‘on the open sea’. νηῒ θοῇ is ‘in a swift ship’ (the dative of ναῦς, written with a diaeresis), πλείοντες is ‘sailing’, uncontracted, and ἐμίμνομεν is ‘we waited for’, the imperfect of μίμνω. Ἠῶ δῖαν is ‘heavenly Dawn’, δῖος ‘heavenly’ as a stock epithet. Antinous says ‘we’, so he was one of the watchers. The unit ends at the comma because the whole sentence would run to five lines.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχον λοχόωντες, ἵνα φθίσωμεν ἑλόντες
αὐτόν·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachon lochoōntes, hina phthisōmen helontes
auton·
sentences.l:
Telemachus lying in ambush for, so that we might destroy, having seized,
him himself;
sentences.i: lying in wait for Telemachus, so that we might seize and destroy him himself;
sentences.n: λοχόωντες is ‘lying in ambush for’, the participle of λοχάω with its vowels left uncontracted, and it takes the accusative Τηλέμαχον. ἵνα φθίσωμεν is a purpose clause: φθίσωμεν is the aorist subjunctive ‘we might destroy’, and ἑλόντες ‘having seized’ is the aorist participle of αἱρέω. αὐτόν is ‘him himself’, the intensive pronoun, and the unit stops at the ano teleia right after it.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄρα τῆος ἀπήγαγεν οἴκαδε δαίμων,
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἐνθάδε οἱ φραζώμεθα λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον
Τηλεμάχῳ, μηδ’ ἧμας ὑπεκφύγοι·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ara tēos apēgagen oikade daimōn,
hēmeis d’ enthade hoi phrazōmetha lygron olethron
Tēlemachōi, mēd’ hēmas hypekphygoi·
sentences.i: but in the meantime some power has led him away home. As for us, let us here plan a grievous destruction for Telemachus, and may he not escape us;
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, and τῆος is ‘meanwhile’ (the epic and Ionic form of Attic τέως). δαίμων is ‘a power’, an unnamed divine force, used when the speaker cannot say which god acted. οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’, with -δε. ἡμεῖς δ’ ἐνθάδε is ‘and we here’, οἱ is ‘for him’ (a pronoun, not the article), and φραζώμεθα is the present subjunctive of φράζομαι ‘devise’, ‘let us plan’. λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον is ‘grievous destruction’, with Τηλεμάχῳ ‘for Telemachus’ added to say who is meant by οἱ. μηδ’ ἧμας ὑπεκφύγοι is ‘and may he not escape us’: ἧμας is ἡμᾶς, and ὑπεκφύγοι is the aorist optative of ὑπεκφεύγω in a wish.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω
τούτου γε ζώοντος ἀνύσσεσθαι τάδε ἔργα.
sentences.tr:
ou gar oïō
toutou ge zōontos anyssesthai tade erga.
sentences.l:
for I do not think,
while he, at least, is living, that we shall accomplish these deeds.
sentences.i: for I do not think we shall ever accomplish our purpose while he is alive.
sentences.n: ὀΐω ‘I think’ takes an infinitive, ἀνύσσεσθαι, the epic future infinitive, middle, of ἀνύω ‘accomplish’, so that the line says ‘I do not think we shall accomplish’. τούτου γε ζώοντος is a genitive absolute, ‘while he, at least, lives’, ζώοντος being the uncontracted participle (Attic ζῶντος) and γε limiting the claim to him. τάδε ἔργα is ‘these deeds’, the business they have in hand.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς μὲν γὰρ ἐπιστήμων βουλῇ τε νόῳ τε,
λαοὶ δ’ οὐκέτι πάμπαν ἐφ’ ἡμῖν ἦρα φέρουσιν.
sentences.tr:
autos men gar epistēmōn boulēi te noōi te,
laoi d’ ouketi pampan eph’ hēmin ēra pherousin.
sentences.l:
For he himself is skilled in counsel and in mind,
and the people no longer at all show favour toward us.
sentences.i: For he himself is skilled in counsel and in mind, and the people no longer show us any favour at all.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς μέν is ‘he himself’, set against λαοὶ δ’ ‘but the people’. ἐπιστήμων ‘skilled, knowing’ takes the datives βουλῇ τε νόῳ τε ‘in counsel and in mind’ (βουλή ‘counsel’, νόος ‘mind’; νόῳ is the uncontracted dative, Attic νῷ). οὐκέτι πάμπαν is ‘no longer at all’, and ἐφ’ ἡμῖν ‘toward us’; ἦρα φέρουσιν is a fixed phrase, ‘show favour’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετε, πρὶν κεῖνον ὁμηγυρίσασθαι Ἀχαιοὺς
εἰς ἀγορήν—οὐ γάρ τι μεθησέμεναί μιν ὀΐω,
ἀλλ’ ἀπομηνίσει, ἐρέει δ’ ἐν πᾶσιν ἀναστὰς
οὕνεκά οἱ φόνον αἰπὺν ἐράπτομεν οὐδ’ ἐκίχημεν·
sentences.tr:
all’ agete, prin keinon homēgyrisasthai Achaious
eis agorēn—ou gar ti methēsemenai min oïō,
all’ apomēnisei, ereei d’ en pasin anastas
houneka hoi phonon aipyn eraptomen oud’ ekichēmen·
sentences.l:
But come, before he the Achaeans gathers
into assembly — for I think he will not let it go at all,
but he will rage, and he will speak among all, standing up,
that a steep slaughter for him we were stitching, and did not overtake him;
sentences.i: But come, before he calls the Achaeans together in assembly — for I do not think he will let it drop, but he will rage, and standing up before them all he will say that we were stitching together a steep slaughter for him and did not overtake him;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγετε is ‘but come’, the plural of ἀλλ’ ἄγε. πρίν takes the infinitive ὁμηγυρίσασθαι ‘to hold an assembly’ (from ὁμήγυρις ‘gathering’), with κεῖνον ‘that man’ (= ἐκεῖνον) as its subject and Ἀχαιούς, here the men of Ithaca, as its object. The dash sets off οὐ γάρ τι μεθησέμεναί μιν ὀΐω, ‘for I think he will not let it go’: μεθησέμεναι is the future infinitive of μεθίημι in the form -έμεναι. ἀπομηνίσει is ‘he will rage’, future of ἀπομηνίω, built on μῆνις ‘wrath’, and ἐρέει is ‘he will say’. ἐν πᾶσιν ἀναστάς is ‘standing up among all’. οὕνεκα ‘that’ introduces what he will say: ἐράπτομεν is from ῥάπτω ‘stitch’, used as English uses ‘hatch’ or ‘weave’ of a plot, φόνον αἰπύν is ‘steep slaughter’ (αἰπύς ‘steep’ is a stock word for destruction), and οὐδ’ ἐκίχημεν is ‘and did not overtake him’ (aorist of κιχάνω).

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ οὐκ αἰνήσουσιν ἀκούοντες κακὰ ἔργα·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ouk ainēsousin akouontes kaka erga·
sentences.l: and they will not approve, hearing evil deeds;
sentences.i: and when they hear of such evil deeds they will not approve;
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’, the Achaeans. αἰνήσουσιν is the future of αἰνέω ‘approve, praise’, and ἀκούοντες ‘hearing’ is a present participle that gives the time: ‘as they hear’. κακὰ ἔργα is ‘evil deeds’. Murray ends the unit with an ano teleia.

sentences.t:
μή τι κακὸν ῥέξωσι καὶ ἡμέας ἐξελάσωσι
γαίης ἡμετέρης, ἄλλων δ’ ἀφικώμεθα δῆμον·
sentences.tr:
mē ti kakon rhexōsi kai hēmeas exelasōsi
gaiēs hēmeterēs, allōn d’ aphikōmetha dēmon·
sentences.l:
lest some evil they do, and drive us out
from our land, and we come to the land of others;
sentences.i: for fear that they do us some harm and drive us out of our own land, and we end up in the land of other men;
sentences.n: μή with the aorist subjunctives ῥέξωσι ‘they do’, ἐξελάσωσι ‘they drive out’ and ἀφικώμεθα ‘we come’ means ‘lest’, a fear. τι κακόν is ‘some evil’, and ἡμέας is ἡμᾶς ‘us’. γαίης ἡμετέρης is ‘from our land’, a genitive of separation, and ἄλλων δ’ … δῆμον is ‘the land of others’, δῆμος being ‘land, district’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ φθέωμεν ἑλόντες ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ νόσφι πόληος
ἢ ἐν ὁδῷ·
sentences.tr:
alla phtheōmen helontes ep’ agrou nosphi polēos
ē en hodōi·
sentences.l:
But let us be beforehand, having seized him, in the country, away from the city,
or on the road;
sentences.i: But let us get to him first, and take him in the country away from the city, or on the road;
sentences.n: φθέωμεν is the aorist subjunctive of φθάνω ‘get in first, be beforehand’, and ἑλόντες ‘having seized’ is the participle that carries the action: ‘let us forestall him by seizing him’, with ‘him’ understood. ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ is ‘in the country’ and νόσφι πόληος ‘away from the city’ (νόσφι takes the genitive; πόληος is πόλεως). ἢ ἐν ὁδῷ is ‘or on the road’.

sentences.t:
βίοτον δ’ αὐτοὶ καὶ κτήματ’ ἔχωμεν,
δασσάμενοι κατὰ μοῖραν ἐφ’ ἡμέας, οἰκία δ’ αὖτε
κείνου μητέρι δοῖμεν ἔχειν ἠδ’ ὅστις ὀπυίοι.
sentences.tr:
bioton d’ autoi kai ktēmat’ echōmen,
dassamenoi kata moiran eph’ hēmeas, oikia d’ aute
keinou mēteri doimen echein ēd’ hostis opuioi.
sentences.l:
and his livelihood and possessions let us ourselves keep,
having divided them according to what is fitting among ourselves, but the house, in turn,
to his mother we would give to keep, and to whoever should marry her.
sentences.i: and let us keep his livelihood and possessions ourselves, dividing them among us as is fitting, and give the house, in turn, to his mother to keep, and to whichever man should marry her.
sentences.n: βίοτον ‘livelihood’ and κτήματ’ ‘possessions’ are the objects of ἔχωμεν ‘let us keep’, a subjunctive of exhortation, with αὐτοί ‘ourselves’. δασσάμενοι is the aorist middle participle ‘having divided among ourselves’ (δατέομαι), and κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’, μοῖρα being ‘portion’. οἰκία is ‘house’ in a plural form; κείνου is ἐκείνου ‘his’, and δοῖμεν ‘we would give’ is an aorist optative. ἠδ’ ὅστις ὀπυίοι is ‘and whoever should marry her’: ὀπυίω is ‘marry’, said of a man taking a wife.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ὑμῖν ὅδε μῦθος ἀφανδάνει, ἀλλὰ βόλεσθε
αὐτόν τε ζώειν καὶ ἔχειν πατρώϊα πάντα,
sentences.tr:
ei d’ hymin hode mythos aphandanei, alla bolesthe
auton te zōein kai echein patrōïa panta,
sentences.l:
But if to you this word is displeasing, but you wish
him both to live and to have all his father’s goods,
sentences.i: But if this proposal does not please you, and you would rather he lived and kept all his father’s property,
sentences.n: εἰ … ἀφανδάνει is ‘if … is displeasing’, ὅδε μῦθος being ‘this word, this proposal’. βόλεσθε is the Homeric βούλεσθε ‘you wish’, followed by an accusative and infinitive: αὐτόν … ζώειν καὶ ἔχειν is ‘that he himself live and keep’, ζώειν being the uncontracted form of ζῆν. πατρώϊα πάντα is ‘all that was his father’s’, the neuter plural of πατρώϊος. The ‘if’ clause waits for its answer in the next unit; this one stops at a comma because the sentence would run past four lines.

sentences.t:
μή οἱ χρήματ’ ἔπειτα ἅλις θυμηδέ’ ἔδωμεν
ἐνθάδ’ ἀγειρόμενοι, ἀλλ’ ἐκ μεγάροιο ἕκαστος
μνάσθω ἐέδνοισιν διζήμενος·
sentences.tr:
mē hoi chrēmat’ epeita halis thymēde’ edōmen
enthad’ ageiromenoi, all’ ek megaroio hekastos
mnasthō eednoisin dizēmenos·
sentences.i: then let us not go on eating up his goods in plenty, to please our hearts, gathering here; instead let each man court her from his own hall, seeking her with bridal gifts;
sentences.n: μή with the present subjunctive ἔδωμεν ‘let us eat’ is ‘let us not eat’, the answer to the ‘if’ clause; οἱ is ‘his’. θυμηδέ’ is θυμηδέα, ‘pleasing to the heart’, and either agrees with χρήματα ‘goods’ or is taken as ‘to the heart’s pleasing’, the sense chosen here. ἅλις is ‘in plenty’, and ἐνθάδ’ ἀγειρόμενοι is ‘gathering here’. μνάσθω is the third-person imperative of μνάομαι ‘woo’, and ἐέδνοισιν is a dative plural, ‘with bridal gifts’ (the suitor’s gifts); διζήμενος is the participle of δίζημαι ‘seek’. ἐκ μεγάροιο ‘from the hall’ is most naturally ‘from his own hall’, as against ἐνθάδε ‘here’; the line does not say whose hall.

sentences.t:
ἡ δέ κ’ ἔπειτα
γήμαιθ’ ὅς κε πλεῖστα πόροι καὶ μόρσιμος ἔλθοι.
sentences.tr:
hē de k’ epeita
gēmaith’ hos ke pleista poroi kai morsimos elthoi.
sentences.l:
and she then might marry
whoever should give the most and come as the destined one.”
sentences.i: and she may then marry whichever man gives most and comes as the destined one.”
sentences.n: ἡ is ‘she’, Penelope, an article-form used as a pronoun, and κ’ is κε. γήμαιθ’ is γήμαιτο, the aorist middle optative of γαμέομαι, said of a woman, ‘she might marry’. ὅς κε πλεῖστα πόροι is ‘whoever might give most’ (πλεῖστα is ‘most’, πόροι the aorist optative of πορεῖν ‘give’), and καὶ μόρσιμος ἔλθοι is ‘and might come as the destined one’: μόρσιμος ‘destined’ is built on μόρος ‘portion, lot’. The closing quotation mark ends Antinous’s speech at the end of the part.
